clue.text: Punctuation mark in line Cosmo translated

indicators.note: translating turns words into another form, so these letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: the two words taken letter by letter as fodder

explanation.surface: A line from Cosmopolitan magazine, translated, contains a particular punctuation mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The semicolon is a punctuation symbol, a dot over a comma, separating clauses.

clue.text: Speaks about a western actor in musical

indicators.note: one word goes about another, wrapping around it on both sides

blocks.note: Alan Ladd, star of the western Shane

explanation.surface: Someone describes a cowboy-film actor appearing in a stage musical.
explanation.walkthrough: Alan Ladd was the Hollywood star of the classic western Shane (1953).
explanation.definitionFit: Salad Days is a long-running 1954 British stage musical by Julian Slade.

clue.text: Parrot, first to mimic a cry of another bird

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the following word is wanted

explanation.surface: A parrot is the first to imitate another bird's call.
explanation.definitionFit: A macaw is a large brightly coloured tropical American parrot.

clue.text: Regain consciousness, fine and well after knockout, by the way

blocks.note: to come to is to wake after fainting
well means healthy, and it comes after the knockout

explanation.surface: A boxer comes round, fine and well after being knocked out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' places the word for well behind the knockout abbreviation; 'Regain consciousness' looks like the definition but is the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an aside introducing an afterthought, an idiom equivalent to incidentally.

clue.text: Spot comic holing short putt

indicators.note: something short is missing its tail, so the last letter goes
comic suggests clowning about, so the letters are tumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A golfer spots a funny moment as someone sinks a short putt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot' looks like a golf-adjacent noun; it is a verb meaning to come across.
explanation.definitionFit: To light upon something is to discover or notice it by chance, an idiom for spotting it.

clue.text: Child molester in prison on Cephalonia

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the words that follow, running across their boundaries

blocks.note: read straight through the end of the first word into the next two

explanation.surface: A child abuser is locked up in a jail on a Greek island.
explanation.walkthrough: Nonce is British prison slang for a sex offender, especially against children; Cephalonia is a Greek island.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a nonce is a paedophile or other sex offender, the lowest rank in prison.

clue.text: Give birth to first of litter in den

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the next word is used
one piece is placed inside another

explanation.surface: An animal gives birth to the first of its litter in its den.
explanation.definitionFit: To calve is for a cow, whale or elephant to produce young, a specific sense of giving birth.

clue.text: I name rhinoceros - wild no matter what the circumstances may be

definitions.text: no matter what the circumstances may be

indicators.note: running wild means out of control, so these letters scatter into a new order

explanation.surface: A zookeeper names a wild rhinoceros, whatever happens.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means regardless of the weather or conditions, i.e. in any event whatsoever.

clue.text: Spill the beans about that in French resort

indicators.note: the first phrase goes about the next item, enclosing it

blocks.note: to let out a secret is to spill the beans

explanation.surface: Someone reveals a secret about something in a French seaside town.
explanation.walkthrough: QUE goes inside LET OU|T. Le Touquet is a seaside resort on the Channel coast of France.
explanation.definitionFit: Le Touquet-Paris-Plage is a fashionable French holiday town, so a resort.

clue.text: Died down then stopped, after opener dismissed

indicators.note: the opener, the first letter, is sent away, as an opening batsman might be

explanation.surface: A cricket crowd's noise died down and stopped once the opening batsman was out.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the opener is the first batsman; dismissing him drops the first letter of CEASED.
explanation.definitionFit: Eased means lessened or abated, a synonym for died down.

clue.text: Relief comes as swelling is reduced round central part of hock

indicators.note: reducing a word cuts it short, so its last letter is lost
only the middle letters of the next word are kept
the shortened word goes round the kept letters

explanation.surface: Relief arrives as a swelling on a horse's hock goes down.
explanation.walkthrough: The hock is a joint in a horse's hind leg; 'Relief' means a substitute worker here, not comfort.
explanation.definitionFit: A locum is a stand-in doctor or vet, providing relief cover for a colleague.

clue.text: They sell irons and balls

blocks.note: surface reading: a golf shop selling clubs and golf balls
setter's reading: irons is slang for firearms, and balls are what old guns fire

explanation.surface: A pro shop selling golf clubs and golf balls.
explanation.walkthrough: Irons and balls point to golf; read them as pistols and shot and the traders are gun dealers.
explanation.definitionFit: Gunsmiths make and sell firearms (irons, in slang) and ammunition such as musket balls.

clue.text: Entirely the responsibility of Old Trafford?

blocks.note: second meaning, read literally: the onus is on a sports stadium

explanation.surface: Something rests wholly with Manchester United's or Lancashire's stadium.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Trafford is a Manchester football ground and also a cricket ground; 'down to' means 'the responsibility of'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means completely or perfectly, as in 'that suits me' this way.

clue.text: Type of necktie a Caledonian produces

blocks.note: Caledonia is the Latin name for Scotland

explanation.surface: A Scotsman shows off a particular sort of neckwear.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascot is a broad cravat-style neck scarf, named after the racecourse.

clue.text: Crime writer in school is representing house

indicators.note: one word stands for, or represents, another, so it takes that word's place

blocks.note: a famous English public school in Surrey

explanation.surface: A crime novelist at a boarding school stands in for his house.
explanation.walkthrough: Charterhouse is an English public school; put IS in place of its HOUSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Leslie Charteris was the thriller novelist who created Simon Templar, the Saint.

clue.text: Trite remark made by chap finally given free rein

indicators.note: only the final letter of the preceding word is kept

explanation.surface: A man allowed to speak freely comes out with a cliché.
explanation.definitionFit: A platitude is a banal, overused saying, a commonplace remark.

clue.text: Hoax victim left most of food girl brought round

indicators.note: most but not all means the final letter is dropped
the girl is brought round from the end to the front of the other pieces

explanation.surface: A prankster's target is left with most of the food a girl brought along.
explanation.definitionFit: An April fool is someone tricked by a prank on the first of April.

clue.text: Peasants set out around noon, by the way

indicators.note: setting things out lays them in a fresh arrangement
the rearranged letters go around the next item

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for noon

explanation.surface: Farm workers set off around midday on their journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By the way' also defined 3-down; here it is the French phrase meaning in passing, used for a chess capture.
explanation.definitionFit: En passant is French for in passing, used in English for an incidental remark.

clue.text: Shopkeeper burst into tears

indicators.note: something burst is broken apart, so the letters fly into a new order

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper suddenly started crying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'burst into tears' is a stock phrase; 'burst' is the anagram signal and 'into tears' the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A stationer is a retailer of paper, pens and office supplies.

clue.text: Freely available religious work described by senior citizen

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to draw round it, so one piece encircles the other

explanation.surface: A pensioner gives an account of a free religious text.
explanation.walkthrough: OAP, old-age pensioner, is British shorthand for a senior citizen; NT goes inside it: O(NT)AP.
explanation.definitionFit: Beer on tap flows from the keg on demand, so the idiom means readily accessible.

clue.text: Sales talk - head of investments trots out a cliché

indicators.note: the head is the top, so only the first letter of the next word counts
out signals letters knocked out of their usual order

explanation.surface: A financial chief churns out hackneyed sales patter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trots out' looks like one verb; 'out' is the signal and 'trots' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a tired saying that all kinds of people exist, a stock cliché.

clue.text: One member the Spanish push forward

explanation.surface: A single member of a Spanish team drives ahead.
explanation.definitionFit: To impel is to drive or urge onward, a synonym for propelling.

clue.text: Shropshire lad initially cast in silly soap

indicators.note: only the first letter of the word before is wanted
to be cast in a show is to be put inside it
silly means foolish and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A Shropshire boy gets a part in a ridiculous TV soap opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shropshire lad' evokes Housman's poem, but 'Shropshire' alone is the definition. Salop is the old name for that English county.
explanation.definitionFit: Salop is the traditional abbreviation and former official name of Shropshire, an English county.

clue.text: Head of ruling party checking on a rota, maybe

indicators.note: only the top, first letter of the next word is used
the party comes behind, keeping a check on what goes before it

explanation.surface: The leader of the governing party inspects a duty roster.
explanation.walkthrough: A rota is literally a wheel going round; a rondo keeps coming back to its theme, so 'maybe' marks the loose definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A rondo is a musical form whose main theme returns repeatedly, much like a rotating schedule.

clue.text: The case for a range of investments?

blocks.note: first meaning: a flat case for carrying papers or drawings
second meaning: the set of holdings an investor owns

explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks for an argument in favour of diversifying; both senses are the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: A portfolio is both a document carrying case and the collection of assets an investor holds.

clue.text: One invading island, part of Asia Minor

indicators.note: an invader gets inside territory, so one piece enters another

explanation.surface: A lone attacker invades an island in ancient Anatolia.
explanation.walkthrough: Iona is a small island in the Scottish Inner Hebrides, home of a famous abbey.
explanation.definitionFit: Ionia was the ancient Greek-settled coastal region of western Anatolia.

clue.text: Hungarian pianist's record? Sounds like it

indicators.note: says the answer is pronounced like the word just given

blocks.note: a list is a written record

explanation.surface: A query about a famous Hungarian pianist's recording.
explanation.walkthrough: 'record' tempts as a disc; here it means a written list.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Liszt was the 19th-century Hungarian piano virtuoso and composer.

clue.text: Left a station, badly polluted, to cross heart of Burundi

indicators.note: badly means done wrong, so the letters come out in a scrambled order
the heart is the centre, so only the middle letter is taken
one piece crosses into the other, sitting within it

explanation.surface: A train left a filthy station on its way across central Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: A train that has pulled out has departed from the platform.
